skills.title: The Munger Rationality Checklist
skills.tagline: Invert the problem, remove ruin, follow incentives, use several mental models, and compare the best alternatives.
skills.whenToUse: Use when a decision is emotionally charged, politically distorted, complex across disciplines, or vulnerable to avoidable stupidity.
skills.source: Poor Charlie's Almanack and Charles T. Munger's 2014 Berkshire Hathaway shareholder-letter essay
skills.sourceAnchor: Elementary Worldly Wisdom, Psychology of Human Misjudgment, USC 2007 address, and Vice Chairman's Thoughts
skills.problemHint: Describe the desired outcome, the feared failure, the people and incentives involved, and the best alternatives currently available.
skills.corePrinciple: Reliable judgment comes from avoiding ruin and obvious folly, then viewing the remaining choice through incentives, psychology, opportunity cost, and a latticework of models from multiple disciplines.

framework.title: Invert
framework.body: List the outcomes that would make the situation a disaster, then identify the behaviors and conditions that reliably produce them.

framework.title: Remove ruin
framework.body: Eliminate paths that can permanently destroy capital, health, trust, reputation, or future options.

framework.title: Follow incentives
framework.body: Map what every participant gains from action, delay, measurement, and advice. Expect behavior to follow the reward system.

framework.title: Run the psychology checklist
framework.body: Test commitment, social proof, authority, envy, reciprocation, deprival, contrast, availability, and combinations of biases.

framework.title: Use a latticework
framework.body: Reframe the problem through economics, probability, engineering, biology, and history. Seek models that disagree.

framework.title: Compare opportunity costs
framework.body: Judge each option against the best alternative, including waiting. Give the scarce resource to the strongest use.

framework.title: State the least stupid action
framework.body: Recommend the action that survives the checks, along with the conditions that would reverse it.

antiPatterns: Using one favorite model for every problem.
Accepting a person's explanation without inspecting the incentive.
Seeking clever upside before removing paths to ruin.
Recommending named securities or personalized allocations instead of decision principles.
skills.outputShape: Return: Inversion; Ruin paths; Incentive map; Psychology check; Mental-model views; Opportunity cost; Least stupid action; Reversal conditions.
skills.closingQuote: It is remarkable how much long-term advantage people like us have gotten by trying to be consistently not stupid, instead of trying to be very intelligent.

skills.title: Invert the Problem
skills.tagline: Solve forward by first identifying the conditions that guarantee failure and systematically avoiding them.
skills.whenToUse: Use when the path to success is vague, a plan has too many moving parts, or preventing failure is more tractable than predicting a winner.
skills.source: Poor Charlie's Almanack by Charles T. Munger, edited by Peter D. Kaufman
skills.sourceAnchor: Talks on elementary worldly wisdom and inversion, with explicit credit to Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi
skills.problemHint: State the desired outcome, time horizon, constraints, and the failures that would make recovery difficult or impossible.
skills.corePrinciple: When success has many causes, failure often has a shorter and more reliable checklist. Turn the problem backward, prevent those causes, then improve the surviving plan.

framework.title: Define failure precisely
framework.body: Describe observable outcomes that count as failure, including slow decay and irreversible damage.

framework.title: Build the failure recipe
framework.body: List behaviors, incentives, dependencies, and assumptions that would reliably produce those outcomes.

framework.title: Rank by severity and likelihood
framework.body: Put irreversible and compounding harms first, even when their probability appears modest.

framework.title: Install avoidances
framework.body: Turn each high-priority failure cause into a constraint, guardrail, owner, or early warning signal.

framework.title: Solve forward
framework.body: With ruin paths removed, choose the simplest positive action that advances the goal.

framework.title: Pre-mortem the result
framework.body: Assume the plan failed and identify what the checklist still missed.

antiPatterns: Using inversion as pessimism instead of a route to action.
Listing vague fears that cannot become safeguards.
Treating reversible inconvenience like irreversible ruin.
Crediting the maxim 'invert, always invert' to Munger instead of Jacobi.
skills.outputShape: Return a failure definition, ranked failure recipe, avoidance checklist, positive next action, and pre-mortem gap.

skills.title: Incentive Audit
skills.tagline: Predict behavior by mapping what the system rewards, punishes, measures, and allows people to rationalize.
skills.whenToUse: Use when stated goals and actual behavior diverge, a metric is being gamed, advice may be conflicted, or an organization keeps producing the same unwanted result.
skills.source: Poor Charlie's Almanack by Charles T. Munger, edited by Peter D. Kaufman
skills.sourceAnchor: The Psychology of Human Misjudgment, reward and punishment superresponse tendency
skills.problemHint: List the participants, stated objective, metrics, compensation, status rewards, penalties, information each person controls, and current behaviors.
skills.corePrinciple: Never expect an exhortation to overpower a reward system. Change what people gain, lose, measure, and can plausibly deny.

framework.title: Name the real behavior
framework.body: Describe what people repeatedly do rather than what the policy says they should do.

framework.title: Map each participant
framework.body: For every actor, list money, status, convenience, career risk, identity, and control of information.

framework.title: Trace metric gaming
framework.body: Identify how someone can improve the measured result while harming the real objective.

framework.title: Find conflicts
framework.body: Mark advisors, agents, and gatekeepers who benefit from a recommendation, transaction, delay, or lack of transparency.

framework.title: Redesign the system
framework.body: Align rewards with long-term outcomes, add balanced measures, shorten feedback loops, and assign consequences to controllable actions.

framework.title: Test second-order effects
framework.body: Predict the new gaming strategy and how the proposed incentive might crowd out judgment or intrinsic motivation.

antiPatterns: Blaming character before inspecting the system.
Paying for an easily measured proxy and assuming the real goal follows.
Ignoring status, convenience, and job security because they are not cash.
Letting a transaction-paid advisor define the decision process.
skills.outputShape: Return: Observed behavior; Participant incentive map; Gaming paths; Conflicts; Redesigned incentives; Second-order risks; One metric to watch.

skills.title: Lollapalooza Bias Check
skills.tagline: Detect when several ordinary psychological tendencies combine to produce an extreme and irrational result.
skills.whenToUse: Use before a high-pressure sale, crowd-driven decision, escalation of commitment, charismatic pitch, crisis response, or unanimous meeting.
skills.source: Poor Charlie's Almanack by Charles T. Munger, edited by Peter D. Kaufman
skills.problemHint: Describe the decision environment, timing pressure, authority figures, group behavior, prior commitments, rewards, losses, and how the choice is framed.
skills.corePrinciple: Extreme misjudgment often comes from several biases acting in the same direction. The interaction is more dangerous than any isolated tendency.

framework.title: Slow the environment
framework.body: Remove artificial urgency, separate the decision from the presentation, and create time for independent thought.

framework.title: Inventory active tendencies
framework.body: Check incentives, authority, social proof, commitment, reciprocation, scarcity, deprival, contrast, liking, and availability.

framework.title: Find combinations
framework.body: Identify which tendencies reinforce one another and what extreme behavior their combination predicts.

framework.title: Create independent views
framework.body: Collect judgments before discussion, seek a disconfirming expert, and assign a credible dissenter.

framework.title: Reframe the choice
framework.body: Remove sunk costs, sales anchors, and identity language. Compare the decision with the best current alternative.

framework.title: Install a circuit breaker
framework.body: Set a delay, evidence threshold, spending cap, or external review proportional to the downside.

antiPatterns: Naming a single bias and declaring the analysis complete.
Treating group agreement as independent evidence.
Letting urgency prevent a reversible pause.
Using bias labels to insult people instead of redesigning the environment.
skills.outputShape: Return a bias inventory, reinforcing combinations, predicted distortion, independent check, reframed decision, and circuit breaker.

skills.title: The Berkshire System
skills.tagline: Design a low-bureaucracy organization where autonomy, trust, capital discipline, and reputation reinforce one another.
skills.whenToUse: Use when designing a holding company, multi-business organization, acquisition operating model, headquarters, delegation system, or succession plan.
skills.source: Charles T. Munger, Vice Chairman's Thoughts: Past and Future, Berkshire Hathaway 2014 shareholder letter
skills.problemHint: Describe the operating units, headquarters roles, managers, capital flows, reporting burden, acquisition process, debt, culture, and succession risks.
skills.corePrinciple: Centralize capital allocation and leader selection, decentralize operations to trustworthy managers, keep headquarters small, use little debt, and let a reputation for permanence attract more owners and operators who fit the system.

framework.title: Define the center
framework.body: Reserve headquarters for capital allocation, chief-executive selection, essential control, and culture. Challenge every additional function.

framework.title: Choose trustworthy operators
framework.body: Select able, owner-oriented managers who need little supervision and want to remain for a long time.

framework.title: Grant real autonomy
framework.body: Give operating leaders clear outcomes, honest information channels, and freedom over methods. Intervene when integrity, capital, or survival is at risk.

framework.title: Allocate capital centrally
framework.body: Make retained cash compete across all units and external alternatives without letting local prestige determine funding.

framework.title: Preserve permanence
framework.body: Avoid unnecessary sales, leverage, and equity issuance. Make commitments credible enough to attract sellers and managers who value stewardship.

framework.title: Protect the virtuous circle
framework.body: Track whether trust is reducing bureaucracy and attracting better people, or whether weak selection is turning autonomy into neglect.

framework.title: Plan succession
framework.body: Specify who can allocate capital, select the next leader, preserve culture, and act when a trusted manager no longer fits.

antiPatterns: Calling neglect autonomy.
Building headquarters functions that manufacture activity and reports.
Rewarding acquisition volume instead of long-term value creation.
Using debt or equity issuance that undermines permanence and trust.
skills.outputShape: Return: Center mandate; Unit autonomy; Manager test; Capital flow; Bureaucracy cuts; Permanence safeguards; Succession design; Virtuous-circle metric.

skills.title: Deserved Trust
skills.tagline: Build relationships and systems by becoming the kind of partner whose promises, incentives, and conduct deserve trust.
skills.whenToUse: Use when choosing a partner, repairing a relationship, designing delegation, negotiating a long-term agreement, or evaluating a culture that claims to value trust.
skills.source: Poor Charlie's Almanack and Charles T. Munger's USC Law School commencement address
skills.sourceAnchor: USC Law School commencement address, May 13, 2007
skills.problemHint: Describe the parties, promises, incentives, information asymmetries, history, vulnerabilities, and what each side needs to entrust to the other.
skills.corePrinciple: The safest route to trust, loyalty, admiration, and cooperation is to deserve them through reliable conduct, aligned incentives, candid communication, and fair dealing over time.

framework.title: Specify what is entrusted
framework.body: Name the money, information, discretion, reputation, time, or vulnerability placed in the other party's hands.

framework.title: Audit the evidence
framework.body: Review conduct under inconvenience, bad news, conflicting incentives, and prior mistakes. Promises matter less than repeated behavior.

framework.title: Align incentives
framework.body: Reduce situations where one party benefits by exploiting information, delay, complexity, or the other's dependence.

framework.title: Make candor safe
framework.body: Create a direct channel for bad news and reward early disclosure and correction rather than cosmetic success.

framework.title: Match autonomy to evidence
framework.body: Grant the widest discretion supported by demonstrated judgment and integrity, with simple checks around irreversible harm.

framework.title: Become deserving
framework.body: State the concrete promise, disclosure, sacrifice, or consistent behavior required from the user, not only from the other party.

antiPatterns: Demanding trust while preserving one-sided incentives or hidden information.
Replacing judgment with surveillance and calling the result a trust culture.
Treating charisma, similarity, or confidence as evidence of reliability.
Forgiving repeated integrity failures because performance is strong.
skills.outputShape: Return: What is entrusted; Evidence for and against trust; Incentive conflicts; Candor mechanism; Autonomy level; Safeguards; How each party can become more deserving.
skills.closingQuote: The safest way to try to get what you want is to try to deserve what you want.
